plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to plan a 5-minute talk around one idea, open it with a promise, structure it so people follow without slides, say it at a pace a stranger can take in, handle a question you didn't expect, and finish on a line people repeat, having rehearsed it 3 times out loud.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14: give that talk to 5 or more people and ask 3 of them what the one idea was; if they all say the same thing, it worked.
plan.horizon28: Later still, around day 28: speak for 10 minutes with a few slides, or give a 2-minute unplanned answer in a meeting and feel it hold together.

picture.name: Taking someone on a hike
picture.line: A talk is a hike you lead: you pick one summit, tell people why it's worth the climb, choose a path they can walk, set the pace, and make sure they reach the top.

chapters.title: Pick one summit
chapters.covers: Why every talk needs one idea, how to find yours in one sentence, and how to cut anything that isn't on the path to it.
chapters.outcome: You can write the one idea of a talk in a single sentence, and name 3 things you'll leave out.
chapters.hook: Chris Anderson's first rule for a TED talk fits in three words. Most speakers break it in minute one.

chapters.title: Open with a promise
chapters.covers: The first 30 seconds: tell people what they'll be able to do by the end, instead of starting with a joke or a thank-you.
chapters.outcome: You can write and say an opening line that tells the room what they will gain from listening.
chapters.hook: Patrick Winston's opening rule: never start with a joke. His reason is practical.

chapters.title: Lay out the path
chapters.covers: A shape people can follow with no slides: where we are now, where we could be, back and forth, then the way there. Includes one fast structure for when you have 10 seconds to think.
chapters.outcome: You can arrange a 5-minute talk so a listener could draw its shape afterwards.
chapters.hook: Nancy Duarte mapped two famous speeches and found the same hidden zigzag in both.

chapters.title: Build it from what they already know
chapters.covers: Starting from the listener's world, not yours: pick examples they recognise, explain every new word in the same breath, and give them a reason to care before the detail.
chapters.outcome: You can explain one idea from your work to someone outside it, using 2 examples from their life, not yours.
chapters.hook: Why does repeating your point 3 times make a talk clearer, not boring?

chapters.title: Set the pace
chapters.covers: Your voice as a tool: speed, volume, pauses and pitch; the 7 habits that make people stop listening; a 2-minute warm-up before you speak.
chapters.outcome: You can say the same sentence 3 ways, pause for a full 3 seconds on purpose, and do a warm-up before you speak.
chapters.hook: Julian Treasure lists 7 speaking habits that make people tune out. Most of us have 2.

chapters.title: When the path gets rough
chapters.covers: Nerves and surprise questions: what to do with your body in the minute before, how to answer a question you didn't expect, and why 'ask, then wait' matters.
chapters.outcome: You can answer an unexpected question in under a minute with a clear beginning, middle and end.
chapters.hook: Matt Abrahams says the spontaneous answer is a skill, not a talent. It has a drill.

chapters.title: Reach the top, and the last line
chapters.covers: Endings that land: paint what life looks like after the idea, the last sentence people take home, why your final slide is never 'thank you', and a 3-run rehearsal plan.
chapters.outcome: You can write a closing line that restates your one idea, and rehearse the full talk 3 times, out loud, to a timer.
chapters.hook: Patrick Winston's last slide was never 'thank you'. What he put there instead.
